read the world by how it reflects and shifts radio. From a $12 chip that

own. Cheap hardware; real signal processing.

❯ project 01
Doppler Motion Radar
Wave your hand and watch its speed appear — the Doppler core inside every radar

$20
beginner
1 weekend
## why this matters

Every radar on Earth starts with one idea: a moving object shifts the frequency of the radio
it reflects. A pocket microwave module like the HB100 transmits a steady ~10.5 GHz tone and
mixes it with the echo, and what comes out is an audio-frequency “beat” whose pitch is
directly proportional to the target’s speed. Amplify that beat, sample it on an Arduino, run
an FFT, and you can read how fast your hand — or a passing person — is moving, in real time.
It is the cheapest possible way to build genuine radar, the payoff is immediate and visual,
and it is the foundation every later project in this guide builds on.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand the Doppler effect, continuous-wave radar, mixing down to baseband, low-
noise audio amplification, and basic FFT-based spectral estimation on a microcontroller
— the literal core of radar signal processing.

→ the job this maps to: radar & sensing engineering — automotive, security / occupancy
sensing, and defense radar groups.
## how it works

Continuous-wave Doppler: The HB100 transmits an unmodulated ~10.525 GHz carrier and mixes
the returning echo with it. A stationary target returns the same frequency (zero beat); a
moving target returns a Doppler-shifted frequency, and the mixer outputs the difference — a
low audio tone.
The Doppler equation: The beat frequency is fd = 2·v·f₀/c. At 10.5 GHz, every 1 m/s of

radial speed produces ~70 Hz of beat, so walking speed (~1.5 m/s) lands near 100 Hz —
squarely in the audio band, which is why a cheap op-amp can handle it.

Amplifying microvolts: The raw IF output is tiny (microvolts to millivolts) and low-
frequency. A two-stage op-amp with band-pass shaping (roughly 20 Hz–3 kHz) lifts it to a
clean line level the ADC can read, while rejecting DC offset and mains hum.

Sampling and the FFT: An Arduino or ESP32 samples the amplified beat at a few kHz and runs
an FFT. The peak bin is the dominant Doppler frequency; convert it back to m/s with the
equation and you have a live speed readout.

Reading direction (bonus): A plain HB100 cannot tell approaching from receding (both shift
the magnitude up). Modules with I/Q outputs, or an added quadrature mixer, recover the sign
of the shift — the same trick higher-end Doppler sensors use.

Why continuous-wave instead of pulsed? CW Doppler is the simplest radar to build: no fast
pulse timing, no high-speed sampling, just a steady tone and an audio-rate mixer output.
The tradeoff is that plain CW gives you speed but not range — which is exactly why project
3 adds a frequency sweep to recover distance.

Why does the signal land in the audio band? The beat is the tiny difference between
transmit and echo frequencies, and for everyday speeds that difference is only tens to
hundreds of hertz. That is a gift: a $0.50 op-amp and an 8-bit ADC are fast enough, because
all the hard 10.5 GHz RF happens inside the module.

Why an FFT over counting zero-crossings? Real returns contain multiple speeds and noise.
Zero-crossing counting collapses that to one number and fails on weak or multi-target
signals; an FFT shows the whole Doppler spectrum, so you can pick the true peak, see
multiple movers, and set a noise threshold.

## build steps
## interview questions
Power the module, find the IF pin

Give the HB100 a clean 5 V and locate its IF output. Wave your hand in front of it and
scope (or listen to) the pin — you should see a faint low-frequency wiggle that tracks
your motion. That confirms the module works before you build anything.
Build the amplifier

Wire a two-stage non-inverting op-amp with a gain of a few hundred and a band-pass shape
(~20 Hz–3 kHz). AC-couple the input to block the module’s DC offset. The output should
swing cleanly when you move in front of the sensor.
Digitize the beat

Feed the amplified signal into your microcontroller’s ADC, biased to mid-rail, and
sample at ~4–8 kHz. Print or plot the raw samples and confirm faster motion gives a
higher-frequency wiggle.
Run the FFT, convert to speed
Use an FFT to find the peak bin, then apply fd = 2·v·f₀/c to get m/s and km/h. Show it
on serial or a small screen. Wave slow then fast and watch the number rise.
Calibrate and threshold

Walk toward the sensor at a known pace (or roll a ball) to check the reading, and set a
noise floor so an empty room reads zero. You now have a working speed-sensing radar —
the exact front end project 2 turns into a speed gun.

❯ project 02
Radar Speed Gun
Calibrate that radar into real mph — clock a passing car or a fastball

$30
beginner
1 weekend
## why this matters

A police speed gun and a baseball radar are, at heart, the project-1 Doppler front end with a
calibrated readout and a display. This build locks down the speed calibration, adds peak-hold
and a clean numeric display, and aims it at real targets: a car going past, a thrown ball, a
bike. The result looks and behaves like a commercial speed gun — but you built the signal
chain yourself and can explain every number on the screen. It is the most immediately
impressive, demo-friendly upgrade in the guide, and a perfect “before / after” with project 1
for content.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You can take a raw sensor and turn it into a calibrated instrument — fixed-point
conversion, peak detection and hold, display integration, and validating a measurement
against a known reference. That instrumentation discipline is exactly what test-and-
measurement and sensor teams hire for.

→ the job this maps to: measurement & instrumentation, test engineering, and embedded sensor
roles — sporting-tech, automotive test, and T&M companies.
## how it works
From beat frequency to mph: The conversion is fixed: speed = fd·c / (2·f₀). Precompute the

constant for your module’s exact frequency so each FFT peak maps directly to km/h or mph
with one multiply — fast enough to update several times a second.

Peak detection and hold: A passing target’s speed peaks then fades as the geometry changes.
The firmware tracks the maximum valid reading over a short window and “holds” it on the
display — exactly how a real speed gun reports the fastest moment of a pitch or a car.

Cosine (angle) error: Doppler measures only the velocity component along the beam. Aim off-
axis by angle θ and the reading is low by cos θ. Aiming nearly head-on keeps the error tiny
— and explains why speed traps are aimed straight down the road.

Antenna gain and range: The bare module sees a few metres. Putting it at the focus of a
cheap parabolic or horn (or even a metal can) narrows the beam and adds gain, extending
useful range and rejecting off-axis clutter — a tangible lesson in antenna directivity.

Display and packaging: An OLED or 7-segment shows the held speed; a momentary button re-
arms it. Mounting the module, amp, MCU, and display in a 3D-printed grip turns the
breadboard into something that reads as a real device on camera.

## interview questions
Lock the calibration constant
Measure or look up your module’s exact transmit frequency, compute speed = fd·c/(2·f₀),
and bake the constant into firmware. Verify on a known mover before trusting it.
Add peak-hold logic

Track the maximum valid speed over a ~1–2 s window, ignore sub-threshold noise, and
freeze the result until a button re-arms it. Test by walking quickly past the beam.
Validate against a reference

Check readings against a phone GPS speedometer in a car (as a passenger, safely), or a
second method for a thrown ball. Aim nearly head-on to minimise cosine error and confirm
the numbers track.
Add a reflector for range

Mount the module at the focus of a parabolic / horn or inside a metal can to narrow the
beam. Note how range improves and off-axis clutter drops — and how aiming becomes more
critical.
Package it

Fit everything into a 3D-printed grip or box with the display on top and a trigger / re-
arm button. Now film it clocking cars or pitches — a clean, legible speed gun you built
end to end.

❯ project 03
FMCW Ranging Radar

Stop measuring speed, start measuring distance — the principle inside adaptive cruise
control

$70
advanced
1–2 weekends
## why this matters

Doppler tells you how fast something moves; FMCW (frequency-modulated continuous-wave) radar
tells you how far away it is. By sweeping the transmit frequency up in a linear “chirp,” the
returning echo is delayed — and because the transmitter has moved on in frequency during that
delay, mixing the two produces a beat whose frequency encodes range. This is the exact
technique inside automotive adaptive-cruise and weather radar, and building even a short-
range version is the leap from “I detected motion” to “I measured the scene.” It is the most
ambitious build here, so the trick is to build it module-based or as the classic coffee-can
radar rather than laying out microwave boards from scratch.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand FMCW theory, chirp generation and linearity, range-from-beat-frequency,
and the FFT processing (range FFT, and range-Doppler if you go further) that underpins
modern radar — the core skill set of automotive and imaging-radar engineering.

→ the job this maps to: automotive radar and imaging-radar engineering — Tier-1 automotive
suppliers, mmWave chip vendors (TI, Infineon, NXP), and sensing startups.

## how it works

BUILD NOTE
Don’t lay out 24 GHz from scratch. Use a chirp-capable module, or build the MIT “coffee-
can” radar at 2.4 GHz — the cantennas and an $8 mixer do the hard RF, so you focus on
the chirp and the FFT.

The chirp: Instead of a fixed tone, FMCW sweeps the carrier linearly across a bandwidth B
over a time T. The wider the bandwidth, the finer the range resolution: Δr = c/(2B). A few
hundred MHz of sweep gives sub-metre resolution.

Range from beat frequency: An echo arrives delayed by τ = 2R/c. During that delay the
transmit frequency has ramped on, so mixing transmit with echo gives a beat proportional to
range: R = c·fb·T/(2B). Closer targets give a lower beat, farther ones a higher beat.

Generating a linear ramp: A VCO or a chirp-capable source (e.g. an ADF4158-driven module)
produces the sweep. Linearity matters: a non-linear ramp smears the range bins, so a PLL or
calibration keeps the sweep straight.

The coffee-can architecture: The classic MIT short-course radar uses two coffee cans as
transmit / receive horns at ~2.4 GHz, a cheap mixer, and an audio interface or SDR to
capture the beat. It sidesteps custom microwave layout while teaching the entire FMCW
chain.

Range FFT and plotting: FFT one chirp’s beat signal and each peak’s frequency maps to a
target range — a 1-D range profile. Stack many chirps and add a second FFT for Doppler,
separating targets by speed as well: a range-Doppler map.

## build steps
## interview questions
Pick your architecture

Either buy a chirp-capable 24 GHz module (least RF pain) or build the coffee-can 2.4 GHz
radar. The module gets results fastest; the coffee-can teaches more. Commit before
buying parts.
Generate and verify the chirp

Drive the VCO / PLL (or enable the module’s sweep) and confirm a clean linear ramp over
your bandwidth on a spectrum view. Linearity here directly sets your range accuracy.
Mix and capture one chirp

Mix transmit with the received echo and record the beat for a single sweep with your SDR
or audio interface. A nearby wall or a corner reflector should give a clear return.
Run the range FFT
FFT one chirp’s beat and convert the peak frequency to range with R = c·fb·T/(2B). Move
a reflector and watch the peak shift to the correct distance — your range profile.
Make a range plot (and go further)

Sweep continuously and plot range vs time as targets move. For the full picture, stack
chirps and add a Doppler FFT for a range-Doppler map — the same output a car’s radar
produces.

❯ project 04
Micro-Doppler Vital-Signs Radar
Read breathing and a heartbeat across the room — contactless, through clothing

$30
intermediate
1 weekend
## why this matters

The same Doppler module that clocks a car can, pointed at a still person’s chest, pick up the
sub-millimetre motion of breathing and the even tinier motion of a heartbeat. These show up
as a slow “micro-Doppler” wobble riding on the radar’s phase; band-pass the signal into a
respiration band (~0.1–0.5 Hz) and a cardiac band (~0.8–2 Hz) and you can pull out breaths-
per-minute and a pulse without touching the subject. It is a genuinely striking demo —
contactless vitals from a $4 module — and it introduces the phase-based micro-Doppler
processing used in gesture sensing, fall detection, and contactless health.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand phase / quadrature processing, micro-Doppler signatures, narrow-band
filtering to separate physiological rhythms, and the limits of motion-based sensing.
This phase-domain RF skill set maps onto biomedical sensing, gesture / presence radar,
and the mmWave presence-sensing products shipping today.

→ the job this maps to: biomedical and contactless-sensing engineering — medical-device R&D,
gesture / presence radar teams, and health-tech startups.

! NOT A MEDICAL DEVICE
This is a demonstration of micro-Doppler sensing, not a medical instrument. It can show
a breathing and pulse rhythm on a plot; it is not validated, not safe to rely on, and
must never be used to make a health decision or to diagnose anyone. Treat it as physics
you can see — not a monitor.

Micro-Doppler from tiny motion: A chest moving even a millimetre changes the radar path
length, which shifts the echo’s phase. Breathing moves the chest ~4–12 mm; a heartbeat
~0.2–0.5 mm. Both appear as slow phase modulation on the returned signal.

Quadrature (I/Q) phase: Reliable extraction needs I and Q channels so you track phase
directly rather than amplitude. A module with I/Q outputs (or an added quadrature mixer)
lets you compute the small chest displacement over time.

Separating breath from heartbeat: Respiration sits around 0.1–0.5 Hz and cardiac around
0.8–2 Hz. Two band-pass filters split the combined motion into a respiration waveform and a
much smaller cardiac waveform you can rate-count.

Why it is hard: The heartbeat signal is tiny and easily buried by body motion and breathing
harmonics. The subject must be still; averaging over several seconds and rejecting large
motions is what makes the pulse emerge.

Reading the rates: FFT or peak-interval analysis on each filtered band gives breaths-per-
minute and beats-per-minute. Plotting the two waveforms live is the demo: a slow rise-and-
fall for breathing, a faster ripple for the heart.

## build steps
## interview questions
Get clean I/Q (or phase)

Use an I/Q-capable module, or add a quadrature mixer, so you can recover phase — not
just amplitude. Verify by slowly moving a flat reflector and watching the phase track
distance.
Amplify and sample slowly

The vitals band is sub-2 Hz, so low-frequency, low-noise gain matters. Sample at tens of
Hz and log to a PC. Sit still in front of the sensor and capture a minute of data.
Filter into two bands

In Python, band-pass ~0.1–0.5 Hz for respiration and ~0.8–2 Hz for cardiac, and plot
both. The respiration waveform appears immediately; the cardiac one needs a still
subject and clean data.
Extract rates

Run an FFT or peak-interval analysis on each band to get breaths-per-minute and an
estimated pulse. Compare breathing to a manual count and the pulse to a fingertip
oximeter to see how close — and how fragile — it is.
Demo it responsibly

Show the live waveforms and rates on screen, clearly labelled as a sensing demo and not
a medical reading. Test how stillness, distance, and clothing change the result.

❯ project 05
WiFi-Sensing Motion Detector
Sense motion through a wall with a $10 chip and no camera

$12
intermediate
1 weekend
## why this matters

You do not even need a radar transmitter to sense motion — the WiFi already in the room will
do it. A standard ESP32 can expose its WiFi channel-state information (CSI): a fine-grained
measurement of how the radio channel between two devices changes. When a person moves, they
perturb the multipath, and the CSI fluctuates in a way you can detect — presence and motion
sensing, through walls, with a $10 microcontroller and no camera. It is the most accessible
entry point into the very active research area of WiFi sensing (the basis of the new
IEEE 802.11bf sensing standard), and it costs almost nothing.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand channel-state information, multipath and how bodies perturb it, time-
series feature extraction (variance, correlation), and the basics of RF sensing without
a dedicated radar. This maps directly onto the WiFi-sensing and wireless-ML work now
moving from research into products.

→ the job this maps to: wireless sensing and ML research / engineering — WiFi-sensing
startups, presence-detection product teams, and academic RF-ML labs.

! SENSE YOUR OWN SPACE
WiFi sensing can detect people through walls — so keep it to your own space. Sensing or
profiling people who have not consented is a real privacy violation (and increasingly
regulated). Build it to understand the technique and monitor your own home, not to
surveil anyone else.

What CSI is: Every WiFi packet is received across many OFDM subcarriers; CSI is the per-
subcarrier amplitude and phase — essentially a fine-grained snapshot of the radio channel,
far richer than the single RSSI number most devices expose.

Why motion shows up: Indoors, signals arrive via many reflected paths. A moving body
changes those paths, so the CSI shifts over time even when transmitter and receiver are
fixed. Stillness gives steady CSI; motion gives fluctuating CSI.

Getting CSI from an ESP32: Special firmware (the ESP32 CSI toolkit) exposes the CSI for
received packets over serial. With another device generating traffic (a ping flood), you
get a continuous stream of channel snapshots.

Detecting motion: The simplest detector watches the variance or rate-of-change of the CSI
across subcarriers; it spikes when someone moves and settles when the room is empty.
Thresholding that gives a robust presence / motion signal.

Toward classification: With labelled data you can go further — distinguishing walking from
a fall, counting people, or coarse room-occupancy — which is exactly where the research
(and 802.11bf) is heading.

## interview questions
Flash CSI firmware

Load the ESP32 CSI-toolkit firmware so the board reports channel-state info for received
packets. Confirm CSI lines stream over serial.
Generate steady traffic

Have another device send a regular packet stream (e.g. a ping every few ms) to the ESP32
so you get a continuous CSI rate. Verify packets and CSI arrive together.
Log and visualise

Capture CSI to your laptop and plot subcarrier amplitudes over time. With the room empty
the traces are steady; walk through and watch them jump.
Build a motion detector

Compute a rolling variance (or correlation drop) across subcarriers and threshold it.
Tune so an empty room reads “no motion” and a person walking reliably triggers — even
from another room.
Push further (optional)

Collect labelled clips (empty, walking, sitting) and train a simple classifier, or test
through-wall range. Document what the CSI can and cannot distinguish.

❯ project 06
Passive Radar
Track aircraft using a transmitter you don't own — bistatic radar with zero emissions

$70
advanced
2 weekends
## why this matters

The most elegant build here transmits nothing at all. A powerful FM or digital-TV station
already floods the sky with radio; passive (bistatic) radar listens to that signal directly
on one receiver and to its echoes off passing aircraft on a second, then cross-correlates the
two to reveal the planes’ range and Doppler. You build a radar that is completely silent —
undetectable, license-free, and powered entirely by transmitters that already exist. It is
the hardest project in the set because it demands two coherent, clock-locked receivers and
real cross-ambiguity processing, which is exactly why it is the standout portfolio piece.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand bistatic radar geometry, coherent multi-channel reception and clock
synchronisation, the cross-ambiguity function (range-Doppler correlation), and direct-
signal cancellation. Coherent multi-receiver SDR and correlation processing are
advanced, in-demand skills for defense, surveillance, and signals work.

→ the job this maps to: defense and surveillance radar, and advanced SDR / DSP engineering —
radar primes, national labs, and signals-intelligence teams.

## how it works

BUILD NOTE
The whole project lives or dies on coherence — two receivers sharing one clock. A
KrakenSDR (five coherent channels) makes this far easier than hand-modding dongles; get
the clock right and the rest is DSP.

Bistatic geometry: The transmitter (an FM / TV tower) and your receiver sit in different
places, so an aircraft echo travels tower→plane→you. The extra path length over the direct
tower→you path encodes the target’s bistatic range; the changing path encodes bistatic
Doppler.

Two coherent channels: One antenna captures the strong direct signal (the “reference”); a
second captures the weak echoes (the “surveillance” channel). Both SDRs must share one
clock so their samples are phase-coherent — otherwise correlation fails.

The illuminator: Broadband FM stations make great illuminators (strong, wideband, always
on); digital TV (DVB-T) is even better where present. You pick a strong nearby station as
your transmitter of opportunity.

Direct-signal cancellation: The direct signal is enormously stronger than the echoes and
will swamp them. Adaptive filtering subtracts the reference from the surveillance channel
so the faint target returns survive.

The cross-ambiguity function: Correlating the cleaned surveillance signal against delayed,
Doppler-shifted copies of the reference produces a range-Doppler map; aircraft appear as
peaks. This 2-D correlation is the heart of passive radar.

## build steps
## interview questions
Lock two receivers to one clock

Use a coherent SDR (e.g. KrakenSDR), or modify two RTL-SDRs to share a single
oscillator. Verify the two channels are phase-coherent — this is the make-or-break step.
Aim reference and surveillance antennas

Point one antenna at a strong FM / TV transmitter (reference) and the other toward the
sky / area you want to watch (surveillance). Choose a strong, steady illuminator.
Capture both channels

Record reference and surveillance simultaneously in GNU Radio. Confirm the direct signal
dominates the reference and the surveillance channel is mostly that same signal plus
noise.
Cancel the direct path

Apply adaptive cancellation to subtract the reference from the surveillance channel,
suppressing the direct signal so weak echoes can emerge.
Compute the range-Doppler map

Run the cross-ambiguity function (existing passive-radar code helps) to correlate the
cleaned echo against shifted reference copies. Aircraft show up as moving peaks —
confirm against a live ADS-B map.

❯ wrap

You don’t need permission — or a transmitter —
to see with radio.

Doppler, FMCW, micro-Doppler, WiFi CSI, and passive bistatic radar are five faces of one
idea: information lives in how the world bends, reflects, and shifts radio. The hardware is
cheap — a $4 module, a $10 chip, a pair of dongles. The skill is in the signal processing:
the mixing, the FFTs, the phase, the correlation. That is exactly the part employers in
automotive radar, sensing, and defense actually hire for.
// the skill ladder
Build them in order and each one hands you the technique the next one needs:
Doppler →FMCW ranging →micro-Doppler →WiFi CSI →passive bistatic

DO THIS
Build even one of these. Screenshot the live plot — a velocity trace, a range profile, a
CSI spike, a range-Doppler map — log the data, and put it on GitHub with a clear README
and an honest note on scope and ethics. One radar reel and one clean repo prove you can
pull real information out of radio.

Full build notes, parts links, and the next field guide go out in The Build List. The
people actually shipping these — and trading coffee-can and clock-locking tricks — are
in Ohm’s Club.
